newsitem.title: UK: Pregnant IRA bombing suspect loses appeal for bail.
newsitem.headline: Pregnant IRA bombing suspect loses appeal for bail.

text.p: Pregnant IRA bombing suspect Roisin McAliskey lost her appeal for bail on Friday while a government minister was at the centre of controversy for effectively calling her "evil scum."

McAliskey, 25, is in prison in London while she fights her case against extradition to Germany, where she is wanted on charges connected to an Irish Republican Army (IRA) bombing of a British Army barracks.

A High Court judged ruled after a two-hour private hearing that McAliskey, the daughter of a former Irish republican member of the British parliament Bernadette McAliskey, must stay in prison. Her baby is due in May.
Her mother, the former Bernadette Devlin, was a key figure in the Irish republican movement of the late sixties and early seventies.

She told Reuters by telephone at her Northern Ireland home that the British government was using her daughter as "some kind of symbol for crushing any last vestige of belief that they intend to treat Irish people, and Irish prisoners in particular, with any kind of decency or dignity."

The prison service said on Thursday that McAliskey would be allowed to keep her baby with her in prison. It said that she would give birth in a hospital outside jail and then take up residence in a special prison mother and baby unit.
Unlike some prisoners, whose cases have caused an outcry in Britain, she will not be manacled while she is in labour, officials have pledged.

But Home Office (interior ministry) minister David Maclean provoked a row when a letter he wrote saying he had no more sympathy for McAliskey than he had for notorious serial killer Myra Hindley was published in Friday's Guardian newspaper.
In reply to a letter from one of his constituents who had written to him complaining about McAliskey's treatment, Maclean wrote:

"When the day comes that the evil scum of the IRA are no longer murdering the innocent and our children are no longer tortured by the Hindleys of this world, then I am certain that when I no longer need all my compassion for the innocent I shall be able to spare some for the perpetrators."
Prime Minister John Major defended Maclean, saying his words had been taken out of context.
But Maclean appeared to have forgotten that McAliskey has not yet been charged with any crime and she denies any link with the IRA mortar bombing of the barracks at Osnabrueck.
Germany has applied for her extradition to face charges connected to the bombing, in which buildings were damaged but no-one was hurt.

McAliskey was arrested in Belfast last November and has become the focus of an ardent campaign by activists who say she has been subjected to "barbaric and inhumane conditions" and that she should be bailed.
Dozens of them, many wearing the Irish national colour green, lined up outside London's High Court, waving banners, while they waited for the judge's decision on Friday.
The prison service says her treatment has been "appropriate and humane".

The IRA called a ceasefire in its battle to oust Britain from Northern Ireland in August 1994, but broke it 17 months later with a series of attacks on targets in mainland Britain before the Osnabrueck attack.
